records.place: Guarilihue, near Coelemu, Itata Valley, Southern Chile

wine.name: Viejas Tinajas Cinsault
wine.grapes: Cinsault alone, from old, ungrafted, dry farmed bush vines.
wine.sites: A heritage vineyard at Guarilihue in the coastal hills of Itata, on granite with some quartz, dry farmed and open to the cool Pacific air; the house's 2018 sheet dates its planting to 1982.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed by hand and the whole berries go into old clay tinajas, which the house calls centennial, where they ferment on their own yeasts in a gentle, semi carbonic manner. The wine is raised in the same tinajas, without any oak, and bottled with little intervention.
wine.glass: Pale, bright ruby; wild strawberry, red cherry and redcurrant over dried roses, a dusty, earthy note of the clay and a touch of white pepper; light bodied, with fine, dry tannin, fresh acidity and a savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Made for its freshness, it is lovely within three or four years of the vintage and holds well for a few more.
wine.serve: 13 to 14 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: Old tinajas: the clay jars, many over a century old, in which the wine ferments and ages.
The denomination of the Itata, a subregion of Chile's Southern region under the wine zoning of 1994.
A designation of the dry inland south; some vintages carried it, as the Itata name was barred for Cinsault until 2015.

records.table: Clay jars more than a century old, and no oak at all, ferment and age De Martino's Viejas Tinajas Cinsault, from old dry farmed vines at Guarilihue in Itata. Pale, dusty and full of wild strawberry, it is a red to drink cool.
records.story: The house counts its years from 1934, when its founder, an Italian immigrant, settled at Isla de Maipo, south of Santiago. The family has run it since, over four generations by its own account. For decades De Martino was a Maipo house of Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère, and it is credited with the first Chilean wine labelled as Carmenère, in 1996. Its turn came with the 2011 vintage, when it made a Cinsault from Itata in old clay tinajas gathered from across the country, the first Viejas Tinajas. The wine came from the dry hills of Guarilihue, where vines have grown since the Spanish settled Concepción in the sixteenth century. Some vintages were sold as Secano Interior, because until a decree of 2015 the Itata name could not be used for Cinsault; since then it carries Itata. Light, clay raised and low in alcohol, it stood against the ripe, oaked style of Chilean export reds. It was the bottle that put Itata Cinsault on export lists, and a clear lesson in what clay does that oak does not.

Tinajas are clay jars, not oak barrels, and they give the wine no wood flavour.
Cinsault in Itata is old dry farmed bush vine country, not the País of the mission vines, though the two grow side by side.

wine.name: Grand Itata Tinto
wine.grapes: Cinsault, by far the larger part, with a little País.
wine.sites: Old, dry farmed, head trained bush vines of the La Bella vineyard on the hills of Guarilihue in Itata, planted in 1960 by the importers' sheets, on granite, farmed with growers whose families have worked them for generations.
wine.making: Picked by hand, the whole berries ferment on their own yeasts in concrete. The wine was raised for about a year in concrete in the vintages whose sheets were read, though some later vintages are said to see old oak, and it is bottled with little added.
wine.glass: Raspberry, sour cherry and pomegranate over dried herbs, rose petal and a stony, granite note; light to medium in body, with soft, fine tannin, bright acidity and a juicy, gently savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young and fresh, within three or four years of the vintage, though a good year holds a little longer.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's name for its Itata wines, a red Tinto and a white Blanco.

records.table: Rogue Vine buys the Cinsault for its Grand Itata Tinto from growers' bush vines of 1960 in the dry granite hills of Guarilihue, adds a little País and ferments it in concrete. Light, juicy and fresh, it is served at 13 to 15 degrees.
records.story: Rogue Vine started in a garage in Concepción in 2011, the work of two founders who had met teaching at the city's university, the Universidad de Concepción, with grapes bought from the Itata hills to the north. The country they turned to is old wine land: vines were planted around Concepción within a generation of the Spanish settlement of 1550, and the law of 1994 that mapped Chile's wine country made the Itata a subregion of the Southern region. By the twenty first century its old Cinsault, País and Moscatel bush vines, dry farmed on granite, were mostly sold by the kilo to large wineries. The founders chose instead to work with small growers in Guarilihue and Nipas, on vineyards they describe as sixty years old and more, some far older, buying from the same families each year rather than owning the land. Their wines are picked early and fermented on native yeasts, at modest alcohol. The Grand Itata Tinto, from Cinsault planted in 1960, became the project's red, beside a Grand Itata Blanco of Moscatel and Riesling. What reaches the glass is the growers' Itata, the old granite hills made light and fresh.

Grand is part of the label's name, not a classification or a rank under Chilean law.

records.place: Traiguén, Valle del Malleco, Southern Chile

wine.name: Sol de Sol Chardonnay
wine.sites: The house's original vineyard at Traiguén in the Malleco valley, south of the Bío Bío, planted in 1993 on deep red clay of volcanic origin with granite, in a cool, wet climate that ripens slowly and keeps acidity high.
wine.making: The bunches are pressed whole and the juice fermented in oak barrels, only a small share of them new, where the wine rests for about nine months. Only a small part goes through malolactic conversion, which keeps its edge.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and white peach over hazelnut, toast and a flinty, struck match note; taut and fresh, with lively acidity, a fine texture and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Good on release, it gains depth over five to eight years and a strong vintage keeps for a decade.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The name as the house prints it: sun of suns, the far southern label of Viña Aquitania.
The southern denomination around Traiguén, a protected name that may be followed by Traiguén.
The town in the Malleco where the vines grow, named on the label beside the valley.

records.table: South of the Bío Bío, at Traiguén in the Malleco, vines planted in 1993 give Viña Aquitania its Sol de Sol Chardonnay, pressed whole, fermented in barrel and kept lean: taut, flinty and fresh, a cool climate white for fish.
records.story: Two Bordeaux winemakers, then the owner of Château Cos d'Estournel and the director of Château Margaux, set Viña Aquitania in motion in 1984, when they began searching Chile for a site of their own. In 1990, with a Chilean agronomist and winemaker of French descent as their partner, they bought land at the Quebrada de Macul, at the foot of the Andes in the Maipo, and the winery there was finished in 1993. That same year the Chilean partner worked with his father in law, a farmer at Traiguén in the Malleco, far to the south beyond the Bío Bío, to plant Chardonnay on his land: by the house's account the first vineyard of the zone. The first wine, Sol de Sol Chardonnay, was made with the 2000 vintage. As the house tells it, the Malleco then had no denomination of its own, and the wine's success helped bring the valley into Chile's wine map. In 2002 a Champagne agronomist and old friend of the founders joined as a fourth partner, and a Sol de Sol sparkling wine followed. The Chardonnay was the proof that Chile's far south could ripen fine white grapes, cool, slow and tense.

wine.name: Pipeño
wine.grapes: País alone, the old mission grape of the Spanish settlers.
wine.sites: The family farm at Yumbel in the dry inland hills of the Bío Bío, its old, dry farmed País vines on trumao, a sandy soil of volcanic ash, as the family describes it.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and ferment on their own yeasts in open vats of raulí, the native southern beech, with no pressing of the skins. The free run wine then rests on its fine lees for a few months in raulí casks, the pipas that give pipeño its name, and is bottled unfined, unfiltered and without added sulphur.
wine.glass: Pale and slightly cloudy; crushed red cherry, cranberry and wild strawberry over a rustic, earthy note of the old wood and a hint of dried herbs; light, juicy and fresh, with gentle, chalky tannin and a short, thirst quenching finish.
wine.ageing: A country wine for its first year or two, drunk young and fresh while its fruit is bright.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, cool from the cellar; no need to decant; a tumbler or a small red wine glass.

label.means: The traditional country wine of southern Chile, named for the pipa, the cask in which it rests.
The dry inland country of the south; a decree of 2015 lets País and Cinsault carry it before the place name.
The town of the family farm, in the Bío Bío, named on the label beside the appellation.

records.table: Cacique Maravilla's Pipeño is the old country wine of the Bío Bío: País from a family farm at Yumbel, fermented in open raulí vats and bottled in a litre with nothing added. Light, juicy and rustic, it is a wine for a cool glass and a long table.
records.story: The family behind Cacique Maravilla has farmed at Yumbel, in the dry inland hills of the Bío Bío, for seven generations, and by its own account its first País vines were planted in 1776, though another account puts the family's vines in the 1760s. The name, as the family tells it, was given to a forebear by the Mapuche of the district, who called him the Cacique Maravilla, the wondrous chief. For most of its history the farm made pipeño, the rough, fresh País of the southern countryside, fermented in open vats of raulí and sold in bulk or drunk at home. The Bío Bío became a subregion of the Southern region under the wine law of 1994, but the old País and its pipeño stood outside the fine wine trade. The present generation turned that around: it bottled the farm's pipeño under the family's name, in a convivial litre bottle, and by the 2014 vintage the Pipeño País was reaching export lists and reviewers abroad. This is pipeño as the south has always made it, given only a bottle and a label.

Raulí is the native southern beech, not oak; the vats and pipas of pipeño are traditionally made of it.
Yumbel is in the Bío Bío, not in the Itata, though both lie in Chile's Southern region.

wine.name: Rivera del Notro
wine.grapes: País alone, from very old vines.
wine.sites: A single old vineyard outside Nacimiento, some eight hundred metres from the Bío Bío river, on alluvial soils over dark sand; the house dates its País to two hundred years and more.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and ferment on their own yeasts. The wine is raised for some months in neutral vessels, steel and in some vintages concrete, with no new oak, and bottled with little intervention.
wine.glass: Red cherry, redcurrant and raspberry over eucalyptus, fresh mint and an iron, earthy note; light bodied and juicy, with firm, slightly rustic tannin, bright acidity and a fresh, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and juicy on release, it drinks well within four or five years, though its tannin carries a good vintage a little longer.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The wine's name, given to both a red País and a white blend of the house.
Spanish for red: the País of the Bío Bío, as against the Blanco.
The Bío Bío Valley, a subregion of Chile's Southern region under the zoning of 1994.

records.table: Outside Nacimiento, close to the Bío Bío river, very old País vines yield Roberto Henríquez's red Rivera del Notro, fermented on its own yeasts and raised without new oak. Cherry and mint over firm tannin, light in body; a little chill suits it.
records.story: País came to Chile with the Spanish in the sixteenth century, and around Concepción and along the Bío Bío it was planted as the vine of the missions and the farms; some of those vineyards are said to be two centuries old. Chile's appellation map of 1994 placed the Bío Bío in the Southern region as a subregion, yet its old País was seen as a grape of bulk wine. The grower behind this house was born in Concepción and trained as an agronomist at the university there, then made wine in Canada, South Africa and the Loire, where he learnt natural wine from a grower of Anjou, and worked beside a French natural winemaker in Chile. In 2015 he went out on his own, back in his home country of the Bío Bío, working old vineyards, many on long agreements with their owners, in the Bío Bío and the Itata near the Nahuelbuta range, dry farmed by organic methods. Rivera del Notro, the red, comes from one of those old vineyards at Nacimiento. País is taken seriously here: the mission grape of the south, made with care, light in body yet with real grip.

others.name: Rivera del Notro Blanco
others.note: A white of the same name, of Moscatel, Corinto (the local name for Chasselas) and Sémillon, by the house.

others.name: Santa Cruz de Coya
others.note: Another País of the house from the Bío Bío.

others.name: País Franco
others.note: A País from own rooted old vines in the Bío Bío.

traps: Rivera del Notro names both a red País from the Bío Bío and a white blend; the red is the one taught here.
País is the same grape as Mission in California and Criolla Chica in Argentina, not a local name for Cinsault.
Nacimiento is a town on the Bío Bío, not a denomination: the label carries the Bío Bío Valley.

questions.exp: He worked in Canada, South Africa and finally the Loire, learning natural wine from a grower of Anjou, before going out on his own in 2015.

report: The house trades under the grower's own name; in prose the person is only the grower, and the Loire grower and the French winemaker in Chile he worked beside, both living, are described, not named.
The founding year 2015 rests on the house's own biography (May 2015) and the South America Wine Guide.
The ageing differs by sheet (steel, concrete then steel, old oak and steel); the record says neutral vessels, no new oak.
The vines' age of two hundred years and more is the importers' claim, told as said to be.
One listing gives the red as Cinsault; the producer's importers and other retailers give País, which the record follows.
The meaning of notro (a native shrub of southern Chile) was not sourced and is left out.

changed: making and table: hand destemming and a year mostly in concrete with a small part in old barrels came from one retailer, and the concrete and barrel figure belongs to the Blanco and the orange wine; the Tinto's sheets give steel, or concrete then steel; now neutral vessels with no new oak.

story and traps[2]: vineyards he rents rather than owns is refuted by the house's own page of its own vineyards; now many on long agreements with their owners; organic and biodynamic without certification narrowed to organic (C Europa); the trap now teaches Nacimiento against the denomination.

others: the Blanco is Moscatel, Chasselas called Corinto and Sémillon by the house, its Itata origin unconfirmed and cut; Santa Cruz de Coya's two hundred years cut; the Pipeño, unconfirmed, replaced by País Franco (two importers).

sources: Afar and wine.com replaced by the house's biography and an importer's sheet; Concepción, the university, the Loire with a grower of Anjou and May 2015 confirmed by the house and Wines Under the Bonnet.
open: The vineyard's soil: alluvial in all accounts, over black basaltic sand in one; the record says alluvial over dark sand.
